THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
Notice of Change (Ch V)  
SECTION 40 – Notice of Change  
➔ Notification and Procedure:  
◆ Employers must follow specific procedures when proposing changes in  
conditions of service related to matters mentioned in the Third Schedule.  
◆ This includes notifying the workers who will be affected by the proposed  
changes.  
➔ Twenty-One Days Notice Period: Employers are generally prohibited from  
implementing the changes within twenty-one days of giving such notice.  
➔ Exceptions to the Rule: There are exceptions to this rule, including:  
● Changes made based on settlements or awards  
● Changes for certain categories of workers covered by specific rules or  
regulations  
 These procedures and exceptions ensure that changes in conditions of service are  
carried out fairly and with consideration for the rights and interests of the workers.  
SECTION 41 – Power of appropriate government to exempt  
If the appropriate Government believes that applying these provisions to a particular class of  
industrial establishments or workers could severely impact the employers and industry, it may  
issue a notification exempting or subjecting them to these rules with specified conditions.  
Voluntary Reference of Disputes to Arbitration (Ch Vl)  
SECTION 42 – Voluntary Reference of disputes to arbitration  
➔ Arbitration Agreement : Employers and workers can resolve industrial disputes  
through arbitration by signing a written agreement specifying the arbitrator(s).  
➔ Handling Even Number of Arbitrators : If an even number of arbitrators are chosen,  
an umpire is designated to break ties.  
➔ Agreement Format and Notification : The agreement must follow a prescribed format,  
and a copy is sent to the appropriate Government and conciliation officer.  
➔ Government Notification : If the Government finds that the majority of parties involved  
agree, it may issue a notification, allowing others affected by the dispute to present their  
case before the arbitrator(s).  
➔ Representation : Representation depends on the nature of the dispute, involving  
negotiating unions, trade unions, or chosen representatives.  
Mechanism for Resolution of Industrial Disputes (Ch Vll)  
SECTION 43 – Conciliation Offers  
The appropriate Government can appoint conciliation officers through a notification to mediate  
and facilitate the resolution of industrial disputes. These officers can be designated for specific  
areas or industries, either on a permanent or temporary basis.  
2
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
SECTION 44 – Industrial Tribunal  
➔ Establishment of Industrial Tribunals: The appropriate Government has the authority  
to establish Industrial Tribunals through official notifications. These tribunals are  
responsible for addressing industrial disputes and related matters.  
➔ Composition of Tribunals: Industrial Tribunals consist of two members, typically one  
Judicial Member and one Administrative Member (person at post of Joint Secretary or  
above).  
➔ Designation of Cases: Cases related to various industrial disputes, including workman  
dismissals and Trade Union disputes, are designated to specific tribunal benches. Each  
bench comprises a Judicial Member and an Administrative Member, with the Judicial  
Member serving as the presiding officer.  
➔ Cases which require a bench of both Judicial Member and Administrative  
Member:  
◆ Application and interpretation of standing order  
◆ Discharge or dismissal of workmen including reinstatement of, or grant of relief  
to, workmen dismissed  
◆ Illegality or otherwise of a strike or lockout  
◆ retrenchment of workmen and closure of establishment  
◆ Trade Union disputes  
Remaining cases shall be entertained and decided by the bench consisting either a Judicial  
Member or an Administrative Member.  
SECTION 46 – National Industrial Tribunal  
➔ Establishment of National Industrial Tribunals: The Central Government has the  
authority to establish National Industrial Tribunals.  
➔ Composition of Tribunals: Each National Industrial Tribunal comprises a Judicial  
Member, who is required to be a former High Court Judge, and an Administrative  
Member, who has been Secretary to Government of India or its equivalent.  
➔ Presiding Officer: The Judicial Member presides over the tribunal.  
SECTION 47 – Decision of Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal  
➔ The decision of Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal shall be by consensus of  
members.  
➔ If members disagree on certain points, they refer these points to the appropriate  
Government.  
➔ Appropriate government will appoint Judicial Member of other Tribunal to hear these  
points and decision shall be taken by majority  
SECTION 48 – Disqualification of members of Tribunal and National Industrial Tribunal  
➔ No one can be appointed or serve as a member of a Tribunal or National Industrial  
Tribunal if they:  
● Are not an independent person, or  
● Have reached the age of sixty-five  
3
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
➔ An independent person" is someone who is not linked to the industrial dispute in  
question or any industry directly impacted by that dispute.  
SECTION 49 - Procedure and powers of arbitrator, conciliation officer, Tribunal and  
National Industrial Tribunal  

Arbitrators, conciliation officers, and Industrial Tribunals follow procedures as per the  
Code and relevant rules.  

Powers Similar to Civil Courts: They possess powers similar to civil courts, including:  
● Enforcing attendance  
● Compelling document production  
● Conducting inquiries  
➔ The costs of proceedings are determined at their discretion and can be recovered as  
arrears of land revenue.  
➔ Awards, orders, or settlements made by these bodies are executed following civil court  
procedures.  
SECTION 50 - Powers of Tribunal and National Industrial Tribunal to give appropriate  
relief in case of discharge or dismissal of worker  
➔ Unjustified Termination: If a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal, during  
adjudication proceedings, finds that the termination of a worker was unjustified, it can  
take the following actions:  
● Order reinstatement with specific terms  
● Provide other suitable relief to the worker  
➔ Interim Relief:  
◆ Additionally, the Tribunal has the authority to grant interim relief to the worker  
during the pendency of the dispute.  
◆ The Tribunal can rely solely on the materials on record without considering fresh  
evidence when deciding on interim relief.  
SECTION 51 – Transfer of Pending Cases  
➔ Transfer of Pending Cases: Upon the commencement of this Code, cases pending in  
the Labour Court, Tribunal, or National Tribunal established under the Industrial  
Disputes Act, 1947, shall be transferred to the Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal  
under this Code.  
➔ Handling of Transferred Cases:  
◆ The transferred cases may be dealt with either:  
● De novo (starting afresh),  
● From the stage at which they were pending before the transfer  
◆ The decision on how to handle transferred cases is at the discretion of the  
Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal  
SECTION 53 – Conciliation and Adjudication of Disputes  
4
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
➔ Role of Conciliation Officers: When an industrial dispute arises or is anticipated, or  
when a notice under section 62 is issued, a conciliation officer will initiate proceedings.  
 The conciliation officer's role includes diligently investigating the dispute,  
encouraging parties to reach an amicable settlement, and reporting any  
settlement.  
◆ If no settlement is reached, the conciliation officer must provide a detailed report  
to the concerned parties and the appropriate Government.  
➔ Timeframe for Conciliation:  
◆ The conciliation officer must submit the report within forty-five days of  
commencing conciliation, with a shorter period for notice under section 62.  
➔ Application to the Tribunal:  
◆ If no settlement is achieved, parties have ninety days from the report's receipt to  
apply to the Tribunal for resolution of the industrial dispute.  
➔ Transition of Presiding Officers:  
◆ A presiding officer from a previously existing Labour Court, Tribunal, or National  
Tribunal under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, can continue as the Judicial  
Member of the corresponding Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal under this  
Code.  
SECTION 54 – Reference and functions of National Industrial Tribunal  
➔ Referral of Dispute by the Central Government: The Central Government has the  
authority to refer an industrial dispute to a National Industrial Tribunal if it deems the  
dispute to involve questions of national importance or if it is likely to affect industrial  
establishments across multiple states.  
➔ Responsibilities of the National Industrial Tribunal: When such a dispute is referred  
or transferred by the Central Government to a National Industrial Tribunal, the tribunal is  
obligated to conduct proceedings promptly.  
➔ Submission of Award: The National Industrial Tribunal must submit its award to the  
Central Government within the specified time frame as per the referral or transfer order,  
or any extension granted by the Central Government.  
SECTION 55 – Form of award, its communication and commencement  
➔ Awards issued by Tribunals, whether composed of both a Judicial Member and an  
Administrative Member, a single Judicial Member, or a single Administrative Member,  
must be in written form and bear the signatures of either or both members, as  
applicable.  
➔ Communication of Awards: These awards are communicated to the parties involved  
and the relevant Government.  
➔ Enforceability of Awards: An award becomes enforceable 30 days after its  
communication unless prevented by the appropriate Government or Central  
Government.  
➔ Grounds for Prevention: The appropriate Government or Central Government can  
prevent the enforceability of an award on grounds of national economy or social justice.  
5
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
➔ Review and Modification: In such cases, they have 90 days from the award's  
communication to either reject or modify it. The modified award becomes enforceable 15  
days after being presented to the legislature or Parliament if necessary changes are  
made.  
➔ Default Enforceability: If no order is issued within the specified timeframe, the original  
award becomes enforceable after 90 days.  
SECTION 56 – Payment of Full Wages to worker pending proceedings in higher courts  
➔ If a Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal orders a worker's reinstatement, and the  
employer appeals to a High Court or the Supreme Court, the employer must pay the  
worker their full wages during the legal proceedings.  
➔ Conditions for Payment: However, this payment is conditional:  
● The worker can't be employed elsewhere during this time.  
● The worker must provide an affidavit to that effect.  
➔ Proof of Alternative Employment: If it's proven that the worker was employed and  
earning adequate income during this period, no wages are payable for that duration.  
SECTION 57 – Persons on whom settlements and awards are binding  
➔ Binding Nature: Settlements agreed upon by employers and workers outside of  
conciliation proceedings, as well as enforceable arbitration awards and settlements  
reached during conciliation proceedings or awards from Tribunals or National Industrial  
Tribunals, are binding on the following parties:  
◆ The parties directly involved in the dispute.  
◆ Any summoned parties (unless summoned without proper cause).  
◆ Extend to: Heirs; Successors; Assigns (for employers); All current and future  
employees (for workers) in the relevant establishment or part thereof  
SECTION 58 – Period of Operation of Settlement and Rewards  
Settlements  
Awards  
Effective Period: Settlements become effective  
upon agreement or signing.  
Effective Period: Awards typically last  
for one year from the date of  
enforceability.  
Government Adjustment: The  
government has the authority to adjust  
the duration of awards.  
Termination: Awards remain in effect  
until terminated with a sixty-day notice  
by a majority party.  
Duration: Settlements are binding for the agreed  
period or six months if unspecified.  
Continued Binding: Settlements continue to be  
binding until a party provides a written notice of  
termination.  
Notice Period: The notice of termination becomes  
effective sixty days after it is provided.  
SECTION 59 – Recovery of money due from employer  
➔ Recovery of Owed Money: Workers to whom money is owed by an employer, whether  
from a settlement, award, or chapters IX or X of the Code, can apply to the appropriate  
Government for recovery, within 1 year from the due date.  
6
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
➔ If the Government confirms the debt, it issues a certificate to the Collector, who is  
responsible for recovering it in a manner similar to land revenue.  
➔ Dispute Resolution: Disputes over the owed amount or benefits can be decided by a  
designated Tribunal.  
◆ The Tribunal typically resolves disputes within three months, although this period  
can be extended with reasons.  
➔ A Commissioner may assess benefit values if necessary.  
➔ Government's Role in Recovery: The Tribunal's decision is sent to the Government for  
the purpose of initiating the recovery process.  
➔ Group Applications: One application can cover multiple workers with similar claims,  
streamlining the process for workers seeking recovery.

SECTION 61 – Certain matters to be kept confidential  
Information obtained during investigations or inquiries concerning a Trade Union or an individual  
business, must remain confidential upon written request by the respective Trade Union, person,  
firm, or company. Unauthorized disclosure is prohibited, except when required for prosecution  
under section 193 of the Indian Penal Code.  
Strikes and Lockouts (Ch Vlll)  
SECTION 62 – Prohibition of Strikes and Lock-outs  

Workers in industrial establishments cannot go on strike or employers cannot declare  
lock-outs without proper notice.  


The notice period for strikes and lock-outs is 60 days.  
Strike or Lock-out cannot start within 14 days of giving such notice or before the expiry  
of date specified in the notice.  


Strikes or lock-outs cannot occur during conciliation, tribunal proceedings, or within 60  
days after their conclusion.  
No notice is needed when there's already a strike or lock-out in progress.  
7
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  


Notification Requirement: Employers must notify the appropriate authority when  
there's an ongoing strike or lock-out.  
Employers must report the notices they receive or give within five days to the  
appropriate Government and the conciliation officer.  
SECTION 63 – Illegal Strikes and Lock-outs  

A strike or lock-out is considered illegal if it begins in violation of the provisions outlined  
in section 62 or if it persists against an order issued under section 42(7).  
➔ Legal Initiation and Ongoing Disputes  
◆ If a strike or lock-out was initiated in compliance with the law and is ongoing  
when an application regarding the industrial dispute is filed with the Tribunal or  
when the dispute is referred to an arbitrator or National Industrial Tribunal, it  
won't be deemed illegal.  
➔ Exceptions  
◆ Additionally, a lock-out resulting from an illegal strike or a strike arising from an  
illegal lock-out is not considered illegal.  
SECTION 64 - Prohibition of financial aid to illegal strikes or lock-outs.  
It is prohibited to knowingly use or allocate funds to directly promote or support any illegal strike  
or lock-out.  
Lay-off, Retrenchment and closure (Ch IX)  
SECTION 65 – Application of Section 67 to 69  
➔ Exemptions for Certain Industrial Establishments : Sections 67 to 69 do not apply to  
industrial establishments covered by Chapter X, those with fewer than fifty workers on  
average per working day in the preceding calendar month, or those with seasonal or  
intermittent work.  
➔ The determination of whether an industrial establishment has seasonal or intermittent  
work is made by the appropriate Government, and its decision is final.  
SECTION 66 – Definition of Continuous Service  
➔ Definition of Continuous Service : Continuous service for a worker means  
uninterrupted employment, even during sickness, authorized leave, accidents, legal  
strikes, lock-outs, or non-fault work stoppages.  
➔ Criteria for Continuous Service : If a worker hasn't had continuous service for one  
year or six months, they can still be considered to have it if  
 In a period of 12 months, the worker has worked for 240 days (190 days in case  
of mine)  
 In a period of 6 months, the worker has worked for 120 days (95 days in case of  
mine)  
8
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
➔ Inclusive of Leave Days : These calculations also include days off due to various  
reasons, such as maternity leave for female workers, laid-off under an agreement, leave  
on full wages, absent due to temporary disablement caused in course of employment.  
SECTION 67 – Rights of workers laid- off for compensation etc.  
➔ Compensation for Laid-Off Workers : When a worker with over one year of continuous  
service in an industrial establishment is laid off (except badli or casual workers), the  
employer must compensate them for laid-off days, paying 50% of their total basic wages  
and dearness allowance.  
➔ Compensation Duration : If laid off for more than 45 days in a year, compensation  
stops unless agreed otherwise.  
➔ Retrenchment Option : After 45 days, the employer can retrench the worker under  
Section 70, and previous lay-off compensation can offset retrenchment compensation.  
➔ Badli Worker Status : "Badli worker" status ends after one year of continuous service.  
SECTION 68 – Duty of employee to maintain muster rolls  
Even if workers are laid off, employers must maintain a muster roll and allow workers to make  
entries when they come to work during regular hours.  
SECTION 69 – Workers not entitled for compensation  
➔ No compensation shall be paid to the worker on lay-off if,  
◆ they refuse suitable alternative employment within the same establishment or  
nearby, offering equivalent wages and not requiring special skills.  
◆ if a worker does not report for work at least once a day during regular working  
hours or  
◆ if the lay-off occurs due to a strike or production slowdown initiated by workers in  
another section of the establishment.  
SECTION 70 – Conditions Precedent to Retrenchment of Workers  
➔ Conditions for Retrenchment : Workers in industries with at least one year of  
continuous service under an employer cannot be retrenched without adhering to specific  
conditions.  
➔ Notice or Wages in Lieu : These conditions include providing one month's written  
notice or wages in lieu of notice.  
➔ Compensation Calculation : Paying compensation equal to fifteen days of average  
pay for each completed year of service or part thereof beyond six months.  
➔ Notification Requirement : And notifying the appropriate Government or designated  
authority as prescribed.  
SECTION 71 – Procedure for retrenchment  
In cases of retrenchment of workers in a specific category, the employer should generally lay off  
the most recently employed worker in that category, unless they have valid reasons to  
choose another worker, which must be documented.  
9
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
SECTION 72 – Re-employment of retrenched workers  
If an employer plans to hire someone within a year after retrenching a worker, Indian citizens  
among the retrenched workers must be given the chance to apply for re-employment and will be  
prioritized over other candidates, as per prescribed procedures.  
SECTION 73 – Compensation to workers in case of transfer of establishment  
When an establishment changes ownership or management, and a worker has served  
continuously for at least one year before the transfer, they have rights similar to those being  
retrenched. This doesn't apply if their service isn't interrupted, the new terms are not less  
favorable, and the new employer is legally responsible for continuous service compensation in  
case of retrenchment.  
SECTION 74 – Sixty day’s notice to be given of intention to close down any undertaking  
An employer planning to close down an undertaking must give a 60-day notice to the  
appropriate Government, explaining the reasons for the closure, except in cases involving  
industrial establishments with fewer than fifty workers or those involved in construction projects.  
SECTION 75 – Compensation to workers in case of closing down of undertakings  
➔ Closure of Establishment : When an establishment is closed down, workers with at  
least one year of continuous service before closure are entitled to notice and  
compensation similar to retrenchment.  
➔ Compensation in Uncontrollable Circumstances : However, if the closure is due to  
uncontrollable circumstances, compensation is limited to three months' average pay.  
➔ Excluded Reasons : Certain reasons like financial issues, stock accumulation,  
lease/license expiry, or mineral depletion in mining operations do not qualify as  
uncontrollable.  
➔ Mining Closure and Alternative Employment : For mining closures due to mineral  
exhaustion, workers can be offered alternative employment within 20 kilometers, with  
similar terms, preventing compensation.  
➔ Construction Projects Duration : In construction projects, if completed within two  
years from setup, workers aren't entitled to compensation.  
➔ Compensation for Extended Projects : But if the project extends beyond two years,  
they can receive notice and compensation for each completed year of continuous  
service exceeding six months.  
Special Provision Related to Lay-off, Retrenchment and closure (Ch X)  
SECTION 77 – Application of this Chapter  

This Chapter applies to industrial establishments with at least three hundred workers  
(or a higher number set by the appropriate Government) on average per working day in  
the past year, excluding seasonal or intermittent work establishments.  
10  
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  


The appropriate Government makes the final decision on whether an establishment falls  
into these categories.  
Industrial establishments include factories, mines, and plantations as defined in  
relevant labor laws.  
SECTION 78: Conditions and Procedures for Lay-Offs  
Employers must obtain prior permission from the appropriate Government for laying off workers,  
except in specific cases such as shortages of power or natural calamities.  
Exceptional circumstances may lead to a temporary exemption from these provisions, and  
alternative employment should be offered to laid-off workers if possible.  
SECTION 79: Conditions and Procedures for Retrenchment  
Employers must obtain prior permission from the appropriate Government for retrenching  
workers who have been in continuous service for at least one year, except in specific cases.  
The worker should be given a three month’s notice in writing giving reasons for retrenchment  
and either notice period should expire or worker has to be paid wages for the period of notice.  
Exceptional circumstances may lead to a temporary exemption from these provisions. Workers  
are entitled to compensation at the time of retrenchment based on their continuous service.  
SECTION 80: Procedures and Conditions for Closure of Industrial Establishment  
11  
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
Employers must apply for prior permission from the appropriate Government at least ninety  
days before the intended closure date.  
Exceptional circumstances may lead to temporary exemptions and workers are entitled to  
compensation at the time of closure based on their continuous service.  
SECTION 81: Duty of an Employer to maintain muster rolls of workers  
Employers in industrial establishments must keep a muster roll and record entries for  
workers who show up for work during normal hours, even if they have been laid off. This helps  
maintain accurate records during periods of layoffs.  
Worker Re-skilling Fund (Ch Xl)  
SECTION 83- Worker re-skilling fund  



The appropriate Government is required to establish a fund known as the "worker re-  
skilling fund."  
This fund consists of contributions from employers, equivalent to fifteen days' wages of  
the retrenched worker, and contributions from other specified sources.  
The fund is intended to be utilized to credit fifteen days' wages to the account of a  
retrenched worker within forty-five days of their retrenchment, as prescribed.  
Unfair Trade Practices (Ch XII)  
SECTION 84 – Prohibition of Unfair Labour Practices  
No one, whether employer, worker, or Trade Union, whether registered under this Code or not,  
may engage in unfair labor practices listed in the Second Schedule.  
Offences and Penalties (Ch Xlll)  
SECTION 85 – Power of officers of Appropriate Government to impose penalty in certain  
cases  
➔ Inquiry and Penalties : The appropriate Government can appoint an officer, not below  
the rank of Under Secretary to the Government of India or an equivalent State  
12  
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
Government officer, to hold an inquiry for imposing penalties under specific sections of  
this Code.  
➔ Inquiry Process: During the inquiry, this officer can summon individuals and request  
documents relevant to the case.  
➔ Penalty Imposition : If the person is found guilty of an offense under the mentioned  
sections, the officer can impose an appropriate penalty.  
➔ Fine for Non-Payment : If the penalty is not paid within ninety days of receiving the  
order, the person may be fined, with the fine ranging from fifty thousand rupees to  
two lakh rupees.

THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
SECTION 87 – Cognizance of Offences  
Legal proceedings for offenses under the code can only be initiated through a complaint from  
the appropriate Government. Additionally, it specifies that such cases must be tried in courts  
with jurisdiction, namely Metropolitan Magistrates or Judicial Magistrates of the first class  
SECTION 89 – Composition of Offences  
➔ Compounding of Offenses: This Section allows for the compounding of certain  
offenses under the code.  
➔ Application for Compounding: An accused person can apply for compounding either  
before or after the institution of prosecution, subject to prescribed conditions.  
➔ Compounding Amount: The compounding sum is typically:  
● 50% of the maximum fine for offenses punishable with a fine only  
● 75% for offenses punishable with imprisonment for up to one year or with a fine  
➔ Utilization of Compounding Amount: The compounding amount is credited to the  
Social Security Fund.  
➔ Exclusions: The provision doesn't apply to repeat offenders or those previously  
convicted for similar offenses within three years.  
➔ Authority for Compounding: The power to compound offenses is exercised by  
specified officers under the supervision of the appropriate government.  
Miscellaneous  
SECTION 90 – Conditions of Service, etc to remain unchanged under certain  
circumstances during pendency of proceedings  
➔ Prohibition on Detrimental Changes: Employers are prohibited from making  
detrimental changes to workers' conditions or punishing them for dispute-related  
misconduct without written permission from the dispute-handling authority.  
➔ Permission for Unrelated Conditions or Non-Dispute Misconduct: Employers can  
modify unrelated conditions or act against workers for non-dispute-related misconduct,  
subject to paying one month's wages and seeking approval.  
➔ Protection for "Protected Workers": The section also protects "protected workers,"  
typically union executives, from adverse actions during disputes.  
➔ Determination of "Protected Workers": The number of protected workers is  
determined as one percent of the workforce, with a minimum of five and a  
maximum of one hundred.  
SECTION 91 – Special provision for adjudication as to whether conditions of service,  
etc., changed during pendency of proceedings.  
Under this Section, if an employer violates Section 90 during ongoing dispute proceedings,  
affected employees can file a written complaint. This complaint is submitted to the respective  
authority overseeing the dispute process, such as a conciliation officer or arbitrator. The  
14  
THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
authority treats the complaint like a pending dispute, adjudicates it, and submits an award to the  
appropriate Government, with the Labor Code's provisions applying.  
SECTION 93 – Protection of persons  
This Code ensures that no person who refuses to participate in or continue a strike or lock-  
out that is illegal under the code will face any adverse consequences such as expulsion from a  
Trade Union or society, fines, penalties, or loss of rights and benefits.  
SECTION 94 – Representation of parties  
This section dictates rules for representation in labor disputes.  
Workers can be represented by  
 any member of the executive or other office-bearer of a registered Trade Union of which  
he is a member;  
 any member of the executive or other office-bearer of a federation of Trade Unions to  
which the Trade Union referred to is affiliated;  
 where the worker is not a member of any Trade Union, any member of the executive or  
other office-bearer of any Trade Union, or by any other worker employed in the industry  
Employers can be represented by  
 association officers or  
 an officer of a federation of associations of employers to which the association is  
affiliated  
 Authorized person in the industry  
Legal practitioners are generally not allowed in conciliation proceedings but may be permitted  
in Tribunal proceedings with consent.  
SECTION 95 – Removal of doubt in interpretation of award or settlement  
Allow the appropriate Government to refer any doubts or difficulties regarding the interpretation  
of an award or settlement to a designated Tribunal or National Industrial Tribunal. After hearing  
the concerned parties, the Tribunal's decision on the matter is considered final and binding.  
SECTION 96 – Power to exempt  
➔ Exemption Authority: Section 96 grants the appropriate Government the power to  
grant exemptions to industrial establishments or undertakings.  
➔ Public Interest Exemption: The Government can also exempt new industrial  
establishments or undertakings from specific Code provisions if it deems it necessary in  
the public interest. This exemption is valid for a specified period from the establishment  
date.  
SECTION 97 – Jurisdiction of Civil Courts barred  
Civil courts have no jurisdiction over matters governed by this Code, and they cannot issue  
injunctions related to actions taken under it.

THE INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS CODE, 2020  
SECTION 99 – Appropriate Government has the power to make rules for the purpose of  
giving effect to the provisions of this Code  
SECTION 101 – Power to amend schedules  
➔ The Central Government can modify or amend the First Schedule, Second Schedule,  
or Third Schedule through a notification. Such notifications are subject to parliamentary  
review. If both Houses of Parliament agree on a modification, it takes effect accordingly,  
but if they agree on annulment, the notification becomes void, while prior actions  
under it remain valid.  
SECTION 103 – Central Government has the power to remove difficulties up to a periof of 3  
years
